title: 6 Best Riding Lawn Mowers in 2026: Tractors and Zero-Turns
metaDescription: The John Deere S120 is the best riding lawn mower for 1 to 2 acres; the Cub Cadet XT1 is the value pick. 6 tractors and zero-turns ranked, with sizing tips.
h1: The 6 Best Riding Lawn Mowers in 2026
intro:
The best riding lawn mower for most one to two acre lawns is the John Deere S120, a 42-inch lawn tractor with a V-twin engine, pedal-controlled hydrostatic drive and the widest dealer network in many regions. The Cub Cadet XT1 Enduro LT42 gives you the same kind of pedal drive for less, and the Toro TimeCutter is the pick for a flat lawn crowded with trees.

Somewhere past three quarters of an acre, a walk-behind stops being exercise and starts eating your weekend. The riding mower that fixes that depends on your slopes, your gates and whether you want to tow. This guide ranks six riders, three tractors, a budget gear-drive model and two zero-turns, then covers tractor versus zero-turn, deck size, transmissions, durable brands, slopes, battery riders, lifespan and cost.
quickAnswer: Buy the John Deere S120 for most one to two acre lawns, the Husqvarna TS 242XD for a heavier build, the Cub Cadet XT1 LT42 for hydrostatic drive at a lower price, and the Troy-Bilt Pony 42 for a flat lawn on a tight budget. Choose the Toro TimeCutter zero-turn for flat ground full of obstacles and the Ryobi 80V zero-turn to quit gas. Any real slope points to a tractor.

Pick the family before the brand. A lawn tractor steers with the front wheels, handles moderate slopes and tows carts. A residential zero-turn pivots in place and mows faster around trees, but it wants flat ground.

For most one to two acre properties, the John Deere S120 and the Cub Cadet XT1 LT42 are the safest buys. Choose the Toro TimeCutter for a flat lawn crowded with beds and trees, and the Ryobi 80V if quiet and no gas matter most.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Riding Lawn Mowers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The order reflects manufacturer specifications (engine, transmission type, deck and warranty), how easy each machine is to get serviced, and themes that repeat in owner reviews and forums. None of these mowers went through hands-on trials for this guide, and the text says when a point comes from a spec sheet or from owner reports.

### Best Overall: John Deere S120 42-Inch
The S120 is the lawn tractor most people picture when they hear "riding mower," and its spec sheet explains the reputation. It pairs a 42-inch deck with a V-twin engine and a hydrostatic transmission run by foot pedals: press forward to go, press reverse to back up, with no clutch and no gear lever. That smooth control is easier on the operator and on the drivetrain, and the V-twin copes with thick grass and moderate slopes better than the single-cylinder engines on cheaper tractors. Because it is a true tractor, it tows a dump cart, sweeper or spreader, and Deere offers front attachments in some markets. The bigger draw is support. Deere's dealer network is the widest in many regions, so service and parts are rarely far away, and the brand's resale value offsets part of the higher price. The deck is stamped steel, so keep it clean, and expect to pay a bit more than for similar hardware from big-box brands.

**Pros:** Smooth pedal hydrostatic drive; V-twin handles load and moderate slopes; broad dealer network; tows carts and sweepers; strong resale.
**Cons:** Stamped rather than fabricated deck; costs more than retail-brand rivals with similar specs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=John+Deere+S120+42+inch+lawn+tractor&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Premium Tractor: Husqvarna TS 242XD
Husqvarna's XD tractors sit a notch above the brand's entry machines, and the TS 242XD is the 42-inch version. Its headline part is a Kawasaki V-twin, an engine family owners often praise for easy starting and long service life. The frame and deck are built heavier than typical entry tractors, which pays off on lots with roots, rough edges and the occasional buried rock. The hydrostatic transmission includes cruise control, so on long straight runs you can set a speed and take your foot off the pedal. The high-back seat is more supportive than most in the class, and owners frequently mention a clean, even cut. The trade-offs are price and service reach: it costs more than comparable Cub Cadet or Troy-Bilt models, and Husqvarna dealer coverage varies, so find out who services the brand near you before you buy. For one to two acres and an owner who plans to keep the tractor a long time, it is one of the sturdier choices.

**Pros:** Kawasaki V-twin; heavier frame and reinforced deck; cruise control; comfortable high-back seat; even cut.
**Cons:** Higher price than entry tractors; thinner dealer coverage than Deere in some areas.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Husqvarna+TS+242XD&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Value Tractor: Cub Cadet XT1 Enduro LT42
The XT1 LT42 brings hydrostatic drive down to a price where many rivals still use gear transmissions, and that alone explains its popularity. Pedal control is easier to learn, gentler on the turf and far more pleasant on a yard full of stops, starts and turns. The 42-inch stamped deck suits one to two acres, and the tractor pulls a light cart or spreader without fuss. Cub Cadet sells it widely through big-box stores, which makes buying and returning simple, while authorized dealers handle warranty repairs. Owners commonly describe it as a dependable, comfortable machine for weekly mowing. The compromises match the price. The transmission is built for light homeowner duty rather than heavy towing or steep ground, and the deck will rust if it is parked full of wet clippings. Keep the deck clean, change the oil on schedule and stay within the manual's towing limits, and it delivers a lot of tractor for the money.

**Pros:** Hydrostatic drive at a mid-range price; sold widely; easy controls and deck lift; handles light tow-behinds.
**Cons:** Entry transmission is not built for heavy towing; stamped deck needs regular cleaning.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Cub+Cadet+XT1+Enduro+LT42&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget: Troy-Bilt Pony 42
The Pony 42 is the least expensive way to get a seat from a major brand. It uses a gear-drive transmission: press the clutch-brake pedal, move the lever to a gear and release. That is simpler and cheaper than hydrostatic, and on a flat lawn mowed in long straight runs it works fine. The catch is that you must stop to change speed, which grows tedious on a lot full of trees, beds and tight turns. The 42-inch deck covers one to two acres, and the tractor is lighter than most competitors, which helps it fit into a small shed but limits what it can tow. Owners generally call it a solid starter tractor for level ground. If your yard has slopes, many obstacles or frequent direction changes, the extra money for a hydrostatic model like the Cub Cadet XT1 is well spent. If the budget is tight and the lawn is simple, the Pony covers the basics.

**Pros:** Among the lowest-priced tractors from a major brand; simple gear drive; 42-inch deck; light enough for small sheds.
**Cons:** Must stop to change speed; basic seat and frame; limited towing.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Troy-Bilt+Pony+42+riding+lawn+tractor&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Zero-Turn: Toro TimeCutter 42-Inch
The TimeCutter is Toro's best-known residential zero-turn, and the 42-inch model fits one to two acres of mostly level grass broken up by trees, beds and play sets. Zero-turn steering spins the mower in place, so trimming around obstacles takes a fraction of the time a tractor needs. Toro's Smart Speed control lets you pick a speed range, slow for tight work near beds or faster for open runs, which helps new operators settle in. A 42-inch deck is compact for a zero-turn, so it passes through many garden gates and fits smaller sheds. Its limits are shared by every residential zero-turn: it is not suited to slopes, because it steers and brakes only through the rear wheels, and it is not built to tow heavy loads. On a flat, busy lawn it can save real time every week. For hills or hauling, buy a tractor; for bigger acreage, see our [best zero turn mowers](/best-zero-turn-mower/) guide.

**Pros:** Pivots in place around obstacles; Smart Speed ranges; compact deck fits many gates; wide Toro dealer and retail network.
**Cons:** Not suited to slopes; little towing capability.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Toro+TimeCutter+42+inch+zero+turn&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Electric: Ryobi 80V HP Brushless 42-Inch Zero-Turn
Ryobi's 80-volt zero-turn puts battery power under a 42-inch riding deck. Brushless motors drive both the wheels and the blades, and a large lithium pack charges from a standard household outlet. That removes gas, oil changes, spark plugs and winterizing from the routine, and it runs far quieter than any gas rider, which owners mention constantly, especially for early-morning mowing. It is sold and serviced through Home Depot. Ryobi rates the mower for a set acreage per charge, but real runtime falls with tall, thick or wet grass, so treat the rating as a best case. On flat lawns of roughly one to two acres it can replace a gas rider outright; on bigger lots, or where the grass often gets long and damp, you may need to split mowing across two charges. The battery pack is the major wear item and costly to replace, so factor it into long-term cost. Like any zero-turn, it is not for steep ground.

**Pros:** No gas, oil or engine upkeep; very quiet; brushless drive and blade motors; instant start; Home Depot service.
**Cons:** Runtime limits acreage compared with gas; expensive battery replacement; not for slopes.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ryobi+80V+HP+Brushless+42+inch+zero+turn&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Lawn Tractor or Zero-Turn: Which Riding Mower Do You Need?
sections.body:
Riding mowers split into two designs, and choosing the wrong one is harder to fix than choosing the wrong brand.

### How they differ
| | Lawn tractor | Residential zero-turn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steering | Front wheels, steering wheel | Rear wheels, lap bars |
| Slopes | Moderate slopes OK | Gentle slopes only |
| Speed around obstacles | Slower | Much faster |
| Towing and attachments | Yes | Limited |
| Learning curve | Minimal | A few sessions |

### When a tractor wins
Lawn tractors are the generalists. Front-wheel steering and more even weight make them steadier on moderate grades. They tow carts, spreaders, aerators and sweepers, and many accept front blades or snow throwers. The cost is speed: wide turns leave more uncut grass around trees to finish with a [weed eater](/best-weed-eater/).

### When a zero-turn wins
On a level lawn with lots of trees, beds and corners, a zero-turn pivots in place and often finishes noticeably sooner. It steers and brakes only through the rear wheels, so it is less stable on slopes, and it is generally not built for towing or ground-engaging attachments.

### The simple rule
Mostly flat, full of obstacles and you only need to mow: look at a zero-turn. Any real slope, or you want one machine to mow, haul mulch and push snow: buy a tractor. For bigger acreage see the [best zero turn mowers](/best-zero-turn-mower/), and if you need a loader, step up to a [compact tractor](/best-compact-tractor/).

sections.heading: What Size Riding Mower Do You Need for Your Acreage?
sections.body:
Deck width should follow your acreage, your obstacles and your gates, in that order.

### Deck size by property
| Deck width | Typical fit |
| --- | --- |
| 42 inches | About 1 to 2 acres with obstacles |
| 46 to 48 inches | About 2 acres, partly open |
| 50 to 54 inches | 2 to 3 acres and up, mostly open |
| 60 inches | Large open properties |

### Why 42 inches suits most buyers
A 42-inch deck clears most garden gates, takes less shed space and turns tightly around trees. If your lawn falls in the one to two acre range with plenty of beds and corners, a wider deck rarely saves time.

### When to go wider
Wider decks pay off on long, open runs. They need more room to turn and a wider gate, and they can be slower on busy lawns. Measure every gate, shed door and path the mower will use, and remember the discharge chute adds several inches.

### Deck build matters more than inches
Stamped decks are common on entry machines and last if kept clean and dry. Fabricated or reinforced decks resist roots and rocks better. On rough ground, a sturdier deck is a better buy than a few extra inches of width. Level the deck at the start of each season using the blade-tip method in your manual to avoid scalping.

sections.heading: Gear, Automatic or Hydrostatic: Which Transmission Is Best?
sections.body:
The transmission is the most expensive part of a lawn tractor's drivetrain, and it shapes how the mower feels every week.

### Gear drive
A manual gear transmission has fixed speeds picked with a lever while the clutch is down. It is cheap and simple, but you must stop to change speed. It suits flat lawns mowed in long straight passes.

### Automatic belt drive
A continuously variable belt transmission gives pedal speed control without shifting. It is a modest step up and fine for light use on level ground.

### Hydrostatic drive
A hydrostatic transmission moves power through hydraulic fluid and gives smooth, infinitely variable speed with forward and reverse pedals. It handles slopes and towing better than belt automatics and is standard on most mid-range and higher tractors. Every zero-turn uses two hydrostatic transaxles, one per rear wheel.

### Which to pick
For most buyers, hydrostatic is worth the extra money. The exception is a simple, flat yard and the lowest possible budget, where a gear-drive tractor like the Troy-Bilt Pony does the job. Whatever you buy, stop fully before switching between forward and reverse, ease onto the pedal on slopes, and respect the manual's towing limits.

sections.heading: Which Riding Mower Brands and Engines Are Most Durable?
sections.body:
Durability comes from the engine family, the transmission, the deck and how easily you can get the machine serviced, more than from the badge on the hood.

### Engines
Small, cheap tractors often use single-cylinder engines; most others use V-twins, which run smoother, handle load better and often last longer. Briggs and Stratton, Kohler and Kawasaki all build residential engines with wide parts support, and Kawasaki and the commercial lines of the others have especially strong reputations. Horsepower figures tell you less than the engine family does.

### Features that make upkeep easier
Look for a spin-on oil filter, an oil drain valve, an easy-to-reach air filter and a fuel shutoff. Owners keep up with service when it is easy, and service is what keeps an engine alive.

### Service network
John Deere has the broadest dealer network in many regions. Toro, Cub Cadet and Husqvarna sell through both dealers and big retailers. Before you buy anywhere, find out which local shop handles warranty work for that model and how far you would have to haul it.

### Fuel
Ethanol-blended gas can go stale in a few months and gum the carburetor. Use fresh fuel and add stabilizer if it will sit more than a month. The off-season steps in our [best gas lawn mowers](/best-gas-lawn-mowers/) guide apply to riding mower engines too.

sections.heading: Can a Riding Mower Handle Hills and Slopes Safely?
sections.body:
Slope rules out more machines than any other factor, and it is where riding mowers cause their worst injuries.

### Know the number
Every operator manual lists a maximum recommended slope, and residential riding mowers commonly fall around 10 to 15 degrees. That assumes dry grass, good tires and careful driving. Check the figure for the exact model, then measure your steepest area with a phone inclinometer app before you shop.

### Tractors versus zero-turns on grades
Lawn tractors behave more predictably on moderate grades because the front wheels steer. Zero-turns steer and brake through the rear wheels and can slide on wet or sloped turf. Neither belongs on a steep bank. Follow the manual's mowing direction, which for most tractors is up and down rather than across, and avoid sudden turns near ditches, drop-offs or water.

### Mow steep spots on foot
If you have to ask whether a slope is too steep to ride, mow it with a walk-behind. A rear-drive [self-propelled mower](/best-self-propelled-lawn-mower/) handles banks a rider should not, and many large-lot owners keep one for exactly that job.

### Everyday safety
Never carry passengers, keep children and pets indoors, and do not override the reverse mowing interlock. Shut off the engine, remove the key and wait for the blades to stop before clearing a clog. If the mower has a rollover structure, keep it raised and wear the belt.

sections.heading: Are Battery Riding Mowers Worth It?
sections.body:
Battery riders have become a realistic choice for many properties, with clear strengths and clear limits.

### Where they shine
They start instantly, run very quietly and need no oil, spark plugs, fuel stabilizer or carburetor work. Charging is usually a matter of plugging into a standard garage outlet overnight.

### Where they fall short
Makers rate acreage per charge in good conditions; thick, tall or wet grass cuts it. Most battery riders suit roughly one to two acres per charge. The battery pack slowly loses capacity and is expensive to replace, often a large share of the mower's original price. Long recharge times can mean finishing a big lawn the next day.

### Who should buy one
If your lawn is flat, within the rated acreage and you value quiet and low upkeep, a battery rider like the Ryobi 80V is a strong choice. For bigger or hilly ground, gas remains more practical. Store the pack indoors at a moderate charge over winter, as manufacturers advise, to help it last.

sections.heading: How Long Does a Riding Lawn Mower Last, and What Does One Cost?
sections.body:
### Lifespan
With regular care, an entry lawn tractor commonly lasts around eight to ten years, and better-built tractors and zero-turns often last longer. Steep ground, heavy towing, outdoor storage and skipped maintenance all shorten that.

### What wears out
Most repairs are wear items, not disasters. Deck and drive belts stretch and crack every few seasons; keep a spare. Blades dull quickly on sandy soil, so sharpen them several times a season. Spindle bearings wear when water gets in. Small starting batteries lose charge over winter and need replacing every few years. Entry hydrostatic transmissions wear faster with heavy towing or steep slopes.

### Seasonal care
At season's end, clean under the deck, change the oil warm, stabilize or run out the fuel, and put the battery on a maintainer. In spring, fit a new air filter and plug, sharpen the blades, grease the fittings and check belts and deck level. Store the mower dry and covered rather than outside under a tarp.

### Cost tiers
Dealers and retailers commonly group riding mowers into three price tiers: entry gear-drive tractors with stamped 42-inch decks, mid-range hydrostatic tractors and entry zero-turns, and premium tractors and upper residential zero-turns with heavier frames and reinforced decks. Most buyers find the best balance in the middle tier, where the Cub Cadet XT1, John Deere S120 and Toro TimeCutter sit. Budget extra for delivery, a spare belt and blades, and any bagger or cart. If fall leaves are a big job, compare a bagger with a [leaf vacuum](/best-leaf-vacuum/) before you buy.

mistakes.title: Buying a zero-turn for sloped ground
mistakes.body: Zero-turns steer and brake through the rear wheels and can lose grip on slopes and wet grass. If your property has noticeable grades, a lawn tractor is steadier, and steep banks should be mowed on foot whatever you ride. Measure your steepest spot with an inclinometer app before you shop.

mistakes.title: Not measuring gates and storage
mistakes.body: A wider deck saves time on open lawns but may not fit through your gate, shed door or garage bay. Measure every opening and path the mower will use, and add the discharge chute, which sticks out several inches past the deck.

mistakes.title: Choosing gear drive for a busy lawn
mistakes.body: Gear-drive tractors make you stop to change speed, which gets old fast on a lawn with many trees, beds and turns. If your yard is crowded, a hydrostatic tractor or a zero-turn is far more pleasant. Save gear drive for flat lawns mowed in long, straight runs.

mistakes.title: Skipping belt and blade maintenance
mistakes.body: Dull blades and worn belts cause most riding mower complaints. Sharpen blades several times a season, keep a spare belt on the shelf, and check belts whenever you hear squealing or see slipping or uneven cutting. Both are cheap next to a week of downtime in peak season.

mistakes.title: Exceeding towing limits
mistakes.body: Overloading a lawn tractor's hitch strains the transmission and can overwhelm the brakes on a slope. Check the manual's towing and tongue weight limits, lighten loads on any incline, and take the flattest route available. A heavy cart pushes the tractor downhill.

faqs.q: What is the best riding lawn mower in 2026?
faqs.a: The John Deere S120 is the best riding lawn mower for most one to two acre lawns, thanks to its hydrostatic drive, V-twin engine and wide dealer network. The Cub Cadet XT1 LT42 offers similar pedal convenience for less money. For a flat lawn full of trees and beds, the Toro TimeCutter 42-inch zero-turn can cut mowing time noticeably.

faqs.q: What are the best riding lawn tractors?
faqs.a: The best riding lawn tractors are the John Deere S120 for all-round use and dealer support, the Husqvarna TS 242XD for a heavier frame and Kawasaki V-twin, the Cub Cadet XT1 Enduro LT42 for value, and the Troy-Bilt Pony 42 for flat lawns on a tight budget. All four use 42-inch decks sized for roughly one to two acres.

faqs.q: What are the best riding lawn mower brands?
faqs.a: John Deere, Husqvarna, Cub Cadet, Toro and Troy-Bilt are the riding mower brands most homeowners shop, and Ryobi leads among battery riders. Deere has the broadest dealer network in many regions, which matters for service. The best brand for you is often the one with a reliable service shop close by, so check local dealer support before buying.

faqs.q: Is a lawn tractor or zero-turn better?
faqs.a: A lawn tractor is better for slopes, towing carts and spreaders, and snow attachments. A zero-turn is better for mostly level lawns with many obstacles, where its pivot steering saves time. Steep areas should be mowed with a walk-behind whichever you choose. Owners of mixed properties often pair a tractor with a trimmer for the edges.

faqs.q: What is the most durable riding mower?
faqs.a: Among the picks here, the Husqvarna TS 242XD is the most durable by spec, with a heavier frame, reinforced deck and Kawasaki V-twin. Durability also depends on care: a hydrostatic transmission used within its towing limits, a deck kept clean, belts and blades maintained, and storage under cover add years to any riding mower.

faqs.q: How long do riding lawn mowers last?
faqs.a: An entry lawn tractor commonly lasts around eight to ten years with regular maintenance, and better-built tractors and zero-turns often last longer. Lifespan depends on hours mowed, slopes, towing, storage and upkeep. Covered storage, an end-of-season service and sharp blades make the biggest difference to how long a riding mower keeps running well.

faqs.q: Is hydrostatic drive worth the extra money?
faqs.a: For most buyers, yes. A hydrostatic transmission gives smooth pedal speed control without shifting, handles slopes and towing better than belt automatics, and makes mowing around obstacles much easier. A gear-drive tractor only makes sense for flat lawns with long straight runs and a tight budget. Try both at a dealer; the difference is obvious within a minute.

bottomLine: Choose the family first: a lawn tractor for slopes, towing and year-round versatility, a zero-turn for flat lawns full of obstacles. Then pick hydrostatic drive unless your lawn is simple and level, size the deck to your gates and acreage, and favor a V-twin if you mow thick grass or tow. For most one to two acre properties, the John Deere S120 and Cub Cadet XT1 LT42 are the safest buys, the Husqvarna TS 242XD suits owners who keep machines for many years, the Toro TimeCutter wins on flat, busy lawns, and the Ryobi 80V is the quiet, gas-free option if your lawn fits its runtime.
